Lessons.Title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem and Similarity
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Identify the three similar right triangles created by dropping the altitude from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse and use matching sides to calculate missing lengths.

Let triangle ABC have right angle C and hypotenuse AB=c. Let D lie on AB with CD⊥AB, AD=x, DB=y, so x+y=c. Triangle ACD and triangle CBD each have a 90° angle at D and share an acute angle with ABC; AA proves both are similar to the original and to each other.

The similarity relations give AC²=c·x, BC²=c·y and CD²=x·y. The first two are leg-projection relations and the third is the geometric mean altitude relation. These hold for nondegenerate right triangles; if one leg is zero, the triangle is degenerate and the constructed altitude logic changes.

Verbal diagram: a right triangle with legs 6,8 and hypotenuse 10 has altitude from the right angle to hypotenuse of length 4.8. The hypotenuse is divided into projections 3.6 next to the 6-unit leg and 6.4 next to the 8-unit leg.

Student task: make a tracing-paper or digital annotation showing all three triangles and ordered similarity correspondences, then use exact proportional equations to calculate altitude and segments. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct right-angle/altitude assumptions, ordered AA matches, valid projection equations and precise numerical verification. Original traced figures and explanations are human scored.

Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 3, CC BY 4.0. Edulytiks wrote all prose and numerical examples independently; protected source graphics and assessment answers have not been copied.

Source 13.1 Similar, Right? (5 min): start by asking whether original source triangle ADC is similar to CDB where CD is an ALTITUDE perpendicular to AB in right triangle ABC. Students identify all three right triangles ABC, ACD, CDB, sketch and trace angle correspondences rather than merely relying on looks. A valid AA proof uses shared/complementary acute angles and right angles; do not treat the two smaller triangles as necessarily congruent.

Source 13.2 Tangled Triangles (15 min): learners trace TWO smaller right triangles onto tracing paper separately, rotate each to match the large triangle orientation, write THREE correctly ordered pairwise similarity statements, label corresponding legs and hypotenuses, and find source side lengths HG, GF, HF from the actual annotated source diagram. Original figure measurements cannot be inferred from the accessible text, so numeric HG/GF/HF must be teacher-verified. Encourage three alternate strategies: Pythagorean theorem, a scale factor, and equivalent ratios; let peers compare correctness.

Source 13.3 More Tangled Triangles (15 min): students independently justify THREE AA-similar triangles ABC, ACD, CBD for an arbitrary right triangle with CD perpendicular to AB, without assuming similarity from image resemblance. Use right angles and complementary acute-angle correspondences to generate many equivalent side-length equations. In consistent source naming, AD/DC=DC/DB and CB/AB=DB/CB, so CD squared=AD*DB, BC squared=AB*DB. Students first compare angle evidence from protractor/tracing with exact reasoning, then group proportional ratios where one side appears twice.

Source 13.3 source numerical extension: Tyler's approximate CB=11.96 from measured/proportional data is challenged by Noah's exact CB=12 using Pythagorean theorem. Explain that approximate ruler/rounded ratios can disagree with exact computed lengths; the original source labelled right-triangle figure must be inspected to justify the exact value 12, not reverse-engineered from the quoted claim. Source synthesis angle BCD=58 degrees, ACD=32 degrees and angle A=58 degrees; in general if BCD=x, ACD=90-x and angle A=x, under the original pictured right-angle configuration.

Source lesson summary: triangle PQR with altitude PS to hypotenuse QR gives AA similarity PQR, SQP, SPR, and two independent geometric-mean/projection examples: when RS=3 QS=7, PS squared=RS*QS=21 so PS=sqrt(21); when PQ=5 QR=12, QS=PQ squared/QR=25/12. Preserve earlier independent 6-8-10 correct model, but make clear the original source's explicit sample values differ and that hypotenuse altitude is a mathematical relation to be justified by AA here, not yet the next lesson's Pythagorean derivation.

Source Practice P1-P7: P1 from triangle ABC right at C with CD altitude, determine which ORDERED triangles ABC, ACD, BCD, BDC, CAD, CBD correspond as written; visual angle-order correspondence, not simply same vertex sets, is crucial. P2 AD12 DB3 yields h squared=36, h=6. P3 a NONRIGHT triangle ABC with CD altitude always has area (h*c)/2, choice D, but its three triangles are not automatically similar. P4 write two valid ordered side-proportion equations for similar quadrilaterals ABCD and A'B'C'D' (previous L12). P5 parallel A'B' missing A'A and B'B requires source image. P6 vertical BC DE numeric AD figure-dependent. P7 midpoint triangle DEF congruence and BC length source-figure-dependent. Original teacher-locked 13.4 Cool-down remains unverified; first-party teacher-reviewed independent altitude diagram plus AA proof and segment-ratio problem are offered.

KeyConcepts.Title: Altitude to hypotenuse
KeyConcepts.Definition: The segment from a right triangle's right-angle vertex to the opposite hypotenuse, perpendicular to it.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Draw it to the interior of hypotenuse for a nondegenerate right triangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Three similar triangles
KeyConcepts.Definition: The two smaller right triangles formed by the altitude are AA-similar to the original and each other.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Match both their right angles and one shared or complementary acute angle.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original ABC (right at C), and triangles ACD and CBD (right at D).

KeyConcepts.Title: Projection formulas
KeyConcepts.Definition: With hypotenuse c split into x,y, legs adjacent to x,y satisfy a²=cx,b²=cy, and altitude h²=xy.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use consistent side correspondence and x+y=c.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute altitude and projections
WorkedExamples.Question: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8 and hypotenuse 10. Find the altitude to hypotenuse and its two projections.
Steps: Projection next to leg 6 is x=6²/10=3.6.
Projection next to leg 8 is y=8²/10=6.4.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each length is positive and h²=xy, consistent with AA similarity.

WorkedExamples.Title: Geometric mean altitude
WorkedExamples.Question: A right-triangle altitude divides its hypotenuse into segments of lengths 4 and 9. Find altitude.
Steps: The right-triangle altitude relation is h²=xy.
Check h/4=9/h=1.5, the expected geometric mean proportion.
WorkedExamples.Check: The whole hypotenuse is 4+9=13 and the leg projections give a consistent right triangle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Justify smaller-triangle similarity
WorkedExamples.Question: Why is triangle ACD similar to original ABC when ABC has right angle C and CD⊥AB?
Steps: Small triangle ACD has ∠ADC=90° by perpendicular altitude.
Both share acute angle at A because D lies on ray AB.
AA proves triangle ACD∼triangle ACB with appropriate vertex correspondence.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The small altitude triangle is similar to the original by AA.
WorkedExamples.Check: One matching right angle and one shared acute angle suffice; the angle at A must be identified.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the wrong hypotenuse projection with a leg.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The leg squared equals the whole hypotenuse times its AD or DB projection adjacent to that leg.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw and label the foot D and associate AC with AD, BC with DB.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the two small triangles are congruent.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: They have common angles but generally different size scales.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use AA similarity and ratios, not equal side lengths unless additional data demand it.

SummaryPoints: A right-triangle altitude to its hypotenuse creates two smaller similar right triangles.
Leg projections and altitude satisfy a²=cx, b²=cy, h²=xy.
Ordered correspondence and hand-drawn representations are teacher assessed.

Lessons.Title: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Prove the Pythagorean theorem from altitude-to-hypotenuse similarity and explain why both the theorem and its converse require the right-angle or matching-side hypotheses.

Let legs be a,b>0 and hypotenuse c>0 in a Euclidean right triangle. An altitude to the hypotenuse splits c into x,y with x+y=c. Similarity gives a²=cx and b²=cy, so a²+b²=c(x+y)=c². This proves the theorem without assuming it in advance.

The converse is also true: a triangle with positive lengths a,b,c satisfying a²+b²=c² and with c the longest side is right-angled opposite c. One can construct a right triangle with legs a,b, whose hypotenuse length is √(a²+b²)=c by the proved theorem; SSS shows it congruent to the given triangle, transferring the right angle.

Verbal diagram: show a right triangle with perpendicular legs a,b, diagonal c, and altitude h perpendicular to c. Label hypotenuse projections x next to a and y next to b. The identity follows by adding the two similar-triangle leg equations.

Student task: write the algebraic proof, draw a separate area-rearrangement illustration of the same theorem, and criticize a nonright triangle mistakenly labelled with c²=a²+b². Teacher rubric (0–4): correct setup, valid similarity equations, algebraic completion and clear necessity of hypotheses. Proof explanations and diagrams require human scoring.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pythagorean theorem
KeyConcepts.Definition: For a right triangle with legs a,b and hypotenuse c, a²+b²=c².
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not use this identity for arbitrary triangles without verifying right angle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Similarity proof
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use the altitude's similar triangles to obtain a²=cx,b²=cy, x+y=c.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add equations and factor c: a²+b²=c(x+y)=c².

KeyConcepts.Title: Right-triangle converse
KeyConcepts.Definition: If three positive side lengths satisfy a²+b²=c² with c longest, they form a right triangle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a constructed right triangle and SSS to transfer its right angle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Similarity-derived proof
WorkedExamples.Question: Prove a²+b²=c² for a right triangle using an altitude to the hypotenuse.
WorkedExamples.Method: Express squared legs with hypotenuse projections.
Steps: Draw perpendicular altitude to hypotenuse c, splitting it into x and y.
AA similarity gives a²=cx and b²=cy.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The Pythagorean theorem follows from similar triangles.
WorkedExamples.Check: The right-angle and nondegenerate hypotheses are used to obtain the altitude similar triangles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test a 5–12–13 triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Side lengths 5,12,13 are given. Determine whether the triangle is right.
WorkedExamples.Method: Apply the converse with longest side 13.
Steps: Positive side lengths satisfy triangle inequality.
The squared-sum equality matches the longest side.
By the converse, the angle opposite side 13 is 90°.
WorkedExamples.Check: It would be wrong to claim the angle opposite side 5 is the right angle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a nonright triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a triangle with side lengths 4,5,6 be right?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare squared shorter sides with longest squared.
Steps: Thus the triangle is not right.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; side lengths 4,5,6 form a nonright triangle.
WorkedExamples.Check: The result follows from the converse condition's contrapositive and correct longest-side choice.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying a²+b²=c² without first establishing a right angle or invoking the converse appropriately.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The formula is specific to right triangles, not every triangle.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify perpendicular legs or use the longest-side squared-sum test for a converse claim.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a proof by assuming a²+b²=c² at the start.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This uses the conclusion as a premise.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Start from AA similarity or an independent area identity and derive the formula.

SummaryPoints: Pythagoras follows from the geometric mean/projection relations of three similar right triangles.
The converse diagnoses right triangles from positive side lengths and longest-side equality.
Exact algebraic proof steps need teacher evaluation, distinct from a numeric question.

Lessons.Title: Finding All the Unknown Values in Triangles
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Select justified proportions, right-triangle formulas and length units to find all unknown sides in similar right triangles, including cases where information is initially insufficient.

A right triangle can be solved from two side lengths using Pythagoras and then related to another by similarity when two angles agree or side ratios are established. The information-gap strategy is to identify the exact needed angle or side correspondence before requesting more numerical data.

Verbal diagram: one right triangle has legs 5,12 and hypotenuse 13. Another right triangle has a corresponding leg of length 15 replacing the length-5 leg. Since scale factor is 15/5=3, remaining leg is 36 and hypotenuse is 39; every ratio stays 3.

Original task: one student holds labelled triangle relationships, another numerical dimensions; without showing the whole card, they must ask targeted questions needed to solve an unknown. Include a deliberately insufficient dataset. Teacher rubric (0–4): useful information request, correct triangle correspondence, accurate computations and unit/condition checks. Original partner communication and reasoning are human-scored.

KeyConcepts.Title: Hypotenuse identification
KeyConcepts.Definition: The side opposite a right angle is the longest side and the hypotenuse.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scaling similar triangles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Corresponding sides in similar triangles share a positive ratio k.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Determine k from a known matching side pair and multiply other sides consistently.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information sufficiency
KeyConcepts.Definition: A solvable triangle problem requires enough valid data to determine the target quantity under the stated theorem.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Ask for a corresponding side or second angle where needed; state uncertainty instead of inventing values.
KeyConcepts.Example: Knowing only one acute angle and the right angle fixes shape but not side lengths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use Pythagoras on a missing hypotenuse
WorkedExamples.Question: Right triangle legs are 5 cm and 12 cm. Find hypotenuse.
Steps: Identify the legs and hypotenuse opposite the right angle.
WorkedExamples.Check: Length cannot be negative; resulting dimensions satisfy the triangle inequality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve a similar larger right triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: The original 5–12–13 triangle is enlarged so its 5-side becomes 15. Find two other sides.
WorkedExamples.Check: All side lengths are in the same units as the given 15.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize incomplete data
WorkedExamples.Question: A triangle is right with an acute angle 40°, but no side lengths are supplied. Can you determine the hypotenuse in cm?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the scale ambiguity inherent in AA similarity.
Steps: The other acute angle is 50° by triangle angle sum.
Many triangles with angles 90°,40°,50° differ by positive dilation.
The hypotenuse could be any positive length consistent with that shape.
A known side length or comparable linear scale must be requested.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No unique hypotenuse length; ask for a side measurement.
WorkedExamples.Check: Angle data establish similarity but do not determine absolute scale.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a shape fixed by angles has a determined physical size.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Infinitely many positive dilations preserve all angles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Request at least one linear dimension before computing actual lengths.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying some target sides by k and others by 1/k.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Inconsistent scale direction violates similarity ratios.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Fix source→target direction and use the same factor for all corresponding sides.

SummaryPoints: Pythagoras determines a missing side in a right triangle from two sides.
Similarity transfers all side lengths by one factor.
Missing data must be identified honestly; peer information-gap reasoning is human assessed.

Lessons.Title: Bank Shot
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Model one-bounce reflection paths and indirect height measurement with similar right triangles, explaining physical assumptions and checking coordinate or measured results.

For an ideal reflection on a straight wall, angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, measured to the normal. A convenient geometric construction reflects the destination across the wall and draws a straight line from the ball to this reflected point. The wall intersection is the calculated bounce point, provided that point lies on the actual wall segment and the path is unobstructed.

Verbal diagram: billiard cushion is horizontal line y=0, ball S=(2,3), intended target T=(8,5), both above wall. Reflect T across y=0 to T*=(8,-5). The straight segment from S to T* meets wall at B=(4.25,0); original path S→B→T has matching absolute approach/rebound slopes.

Indirect measurement with a flat mirror on level ground: assuming equal reflection angles and straight rays, similar right triangles compare object height H over horizontal mirror-to-object distance d1 with observer eye height h over mirror-to-eye distance d2, so H/d1=h/d2. State the mirror alignment, level-ground and observer-position assumptions.

Student task: construct a bank-shot path on a coordinate board and a hypothetical mirror-height estimate, then explain when the reflection approximation is inappropriate (ball radius, friction, offset cushion, uneven ground). Teacher rubric (0–4): correct reflected target, wall intersection, proportion/angle justification and physical limitation. Pool-table paths and mirror measurements require teacher-scored evidence.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reflection path construction
KeyConcepts.Definition: A one-bounce ideal path between start and target reflecting off a straight wall can be made by reflecting the target across the wall.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Draw line to reflected target and take its intersection with the wall, if the point is physically reachable.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal-angle law
KeyConcepts.Definition: For ideal specular reflection, incidence and reflection angles to the surface normal are equal.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check incoming and outgoing line slopes relative to the wall and their angles with the perpendicular.
KeyConcepts.Example: A slope magnitude 4/3 before the bounce equals the rebound slope magnitude 4/3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Indirect measurement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Similar triangles relate height and horizontal distance for reflected sightlines over level ground under valid mirror geometry.
KeyConcepts.Example: Eye height 1.6 m, mirror 1 m from eye and 5 m from object implies H=8 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute an exact bank-shot point
WorkedExamples.Question: S=(2,3), T=(8,5), wall y=0. Find a one-bounce point B under ideal reflection.
WorkedExamples.Method: Reflect target and intersect straight segment with wall.
Steps: Mirror target T across y=0 to T*=(8,-5).
WorkedExamples.Check: Incoming slope -3/2.25=-4/3 and outgoing slope 5/3.75=4/3, giving equal incidence/reflection angles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate building height with mirror
WorkedExamples.Question: On level ground an observer's eye is 1.6 m high, mirror 1 m from observer and 5 m from building. Estimate building height assuming ideal reflected sightline.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the similar right triangles formed by mirror and vertical object/eye lines.
Steps: The observer and building vertical segments form similar right triangles with the mirror vertex.
Set H/5=1.6/1 using lengths in metres.
Check geometry assumes horizontal level ground and correctly placed small flat mirror.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Building height approximately 8 m under the stated idealized assumptions.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is model output, not measured structural height; actual precision needs onsite measurements.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject an unreachable bounce
WorkedExamples.Question: Ideal reflection calculation gives B=(4.25,0) but the usable cushion exists only for 0≤x≤4. Can this one-bounce shot use that cushion?
WorkedExamples.Method: Check the intersection against the finite wall domain.
Steps: The actual wall segment ends at x=4.
Therefore B lies outside the permitted segment.
The ideal infinite-wall solution is not physically available on this finite cushion.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, that ideal one-bounce solution is infeasible for the stated wall segment.
WorkedExamples.Check: A valid path must meet both the geometric angle condition and boundary constraints.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reflecting the starting point and target both and using their direct segment without checking the bounce location.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It may produce no crossing on the intended finite wall segment.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Reflect one endpoint consistently and verify the actual intersection is within the wall bounds.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inferring a measured building height without specifying eye height, mirror distances and level-ground assumptions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Missing distances or nonlevel ground invalidate the similar triangles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record measured inputs, units, sightline geometry and uncertainty before computing.

SummaryPoints: A reflected endpoint reduces an ideal bank shot to a straight-line intersection problem.
Similar triangles support mirror-based indirect measurement under explicit assumptions.
Authentic physical experiments, billiard paths and reasoning require teacher review.
